_about.purpose: Which expanded-octet valences are legitimate, and under what ligands. Consulted only when an atom's valence is not already in RDKit's list for that element, so this file is a set of exceptions, not a valence table.
_about.why_data_and_not_code: Same call the regulatory rulesets made: adding an element is a data edit, and every verdict can cite the rule that produced it rather than a branch in a function.
_about.convention: The lambda-convention (IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Chemistry, Recommendations and Preferred Names 2013, P-14.1) names these states -- lambda-3, lambda-5 and lambda-7 iodanes and so on. The permitted_valences lists below follow it: a hypervalent centre gains ligands in pairs, so the halogens step 1, 3, 5, 7 and never reach an even count.
_about.what_is_actually_verified: The examples named against each element are real, characterised compounds; they are the evidence for the maximum_valence given. The reference line names the convention that organises them. No page-level citation is claimed for a specific number, and nothing here was taken from a source this project has not read -- where a case could not be justified that way (silicon in hexafluorosilicate, boron ate-complexes) the element was left out rather than guessed at.
_about.expanded_octet_requires_ligands: An expanded octet is stabilised by electronegative substituents. That is the whole reason IF7 exists and I(CH3)7 does not, and it is what makes the ligand list a real test rather than a formality.
